title: Dancing before the ark (2 Samuel 6:12–16)
hookLine: the king dances with all his might, and his wife is embarrassed
tomorrow: A seat at the king's table
last: SWIFTER THAN EAGLES, STRONGER THAN LIONS.

cards: Six paces. That's how far the bearers carry it before David sacrifices oxen and fatlings, the King James says. David is king now, bringing the ark of God, the sacred chest of the covenant, up into Jerusalem, his new city.
And out ahead of everyone, the king is not walking with dignity. He's leaping and dancing, the text says, in a plain linen garment.
Above the street, at a palace window, one person is watching who is not dancing at all: his wife Michal, the daughter of Saul.

teach.b: Here is the verse: "And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod." With all his might.
The King James uses the same English words for Samson bringing down the pillars, though the Hebrew behind them differs; here they describe a king's joy.

The linen ephod was a simple garment, the kind the boy Samuel wore while serving at the sanctuary. The text says nothing here of a king's robe, and some readers see a king dressed for service, not for show.
Then the window: "Michal Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart."
It's easy to make Michal the villain, and the text is fairer than that. She loved David once. She saved his life by letting him down through a window.
Then she was given to another man while David was away, and brought back later. Her father and brothers are dead. She has her own reasons to watch from a window.
But when she meets David, she mocks him for uncovering himself before the servant girls like a fool. David answers: it was before the LORD.
"I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight." Sillier still, if that's what worship takes.
Some Christians read this as permission for joy that looks undignified: hands raised, clapping, dancing in church. Others hear a quieter point about the heart: what matters is who the dance is for.
Either way, the king forgot to look like a king.

how: Some churches point to David dancing before the ark when they welcome dance, clapping and raised hands in worship, while others read it mainly as a lesson about humility and the heart behind worship.

o: a plain linen garment worn in service
a royal robe worn on a coronation day
a box carried on poles, like the ark

games.q: the ark comes to Jerusalem — tap the pairs.

s: the text says David danced in his royal robes
it says he was girded with a linen ephod, a plain linen garment (2 Samuel 6:14).
the text calls her Michal Saul's daughter as she watches from the window.
David apologized for how he danced
he said he would be more vile than thus, because it was before the LORD.

games.q: you're David. your wife says you made a fool of yourself dancing in the street. what do you say?
o: you're right. it won't happen again.
it was before the LORD, and I'll be even more undignified.
games.why: "I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight." the dance was for God, not for the window.

practice: If you can stand, stand; if not, stay where you are, and let a song with joy in it play in your head. Move something, your hands, your feet, small and silly is fine, without checking how it looks.
If you pray, make it a dance before God, as David did; if you don't, let it be a dance of thanks for being alive today.

wordCard.voice: Ephod. The plain linen garment David wore as he leapt and danced with all his might before the ark.

orig.note: Hebrew: ephod, a linen garment worn in the service of the sanctuary; David danced girded with one (2 Samuel 6:14).
